subject: lighthouse
pitch: A lighthouse on a tiny island.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module to build a small island diorama with a lighthouse on top, sized realistically at around 20 meters wide for the island and roughly 12 meters tall for the lighthouse, with everything positioned so the base sits at ground level.

I'm sketching out the construction approach: lathe shapes for the tapered tower, gallery, and lantern dome, painted with stripes and colors, plus an irregular rocky island base with scattered boulders and maybe a tiny cottage to round out the scene. I'm reviewing the builder API, starting with how joints are defined with position, direction, and parent relationships.

For stripes I'll use axis "y" so bands wrap horizontally around the tower, alternating red and white; could also try a custom paint function banding by vertical position for a sharper checker look. For the lantern glass I'll just use a simple warm color string, and for the gallery railing I'm considering a ring of repeated elements.

Working out the railing geometry now: using a ring arranged around a vertical frame, with each item spawning a rod from its position outward to form a post, sized to the gallery radius and spaced in a 16-count circle.

For the connecting rail itself, I'm considering a lathe-generated ring band — a small rectangular profile revolved around the vertical axis at the gallery height to form a continuous rail, then extending similar lathe logic for the deck profile stepping outward from the center.

Now I'm designing the island's rock base as a lathe profile, checking that the lowest point doesn't sink more than 2% of the overall model height (roughly 0.28m for a ~14m structure), and adjusting the radius/height points so the island silhouette tapers naturally from a shallow base up through a rounded rocky top around 2m high.

For coloring, I'm applying a countershade gradient from grassy green on upward-facing surfaces to rocky grey on the sides, blending based on surface normal. I'm also planning scattered dodecahedron pebbles along the shoreline rim.

For the tower itself, I'm sketching a tapered lathe profile starting at the island top, narrowing gradually from a 2.0 radius base to about 1.3 at roughly 11m height, considering whether to apply lathe smoothing to round the transitions.

Now I'm deciding on lathe segment count — keeping the default around 12-14 for smooth shading without overdoing part limits. For the exterior, I'm setting up red-and-white stripe bands along the tower's y-axis using a stripe function with some width variation, noting that the taper's noise will naturally wobble the band edges. Finally, I'm starting to block out a small gallery platform lathe profile at the tower's top.

Now I'm designing the lantern room on top—a glowing glass cylinder with dark mullion rods around it, then shaping the roof above as a tapered dome lathe profile.

For the finial I need to use a spike primitive, but since sweeps require an explicit color option, I'll pass that in. Then I'm working out how the gallery deck, railing height, and lantern base all stack cleanly on top of each other at 13.3.

Now I'm adding a keeper's cottage near the island base using a box for the walls and a four-sided cone rotated 45 degrees to form a simple pyramidal roof, sizing the cone radius so the square roof slightly overhangs the box below.

I'm placing a small door and window on the cottage's front face as thin boxes, then scattering a few dodecahedron rocks near the shoreline, some partially sunk into the ground. I'm also considering adding a large flat circular water plane around the island to represent the surrounding sea.

Rotation takes a Vector3 in degrees, good to know. I'll skip extra details like grass tufts, paths, or beacon glow to save time, and start sketching the module structure with imports and the builder setup for the lighthouse, beginning with the root joint.

I'm double-checking the lathe function's signature and outline point requirements—x must stay non-negative, and the island's lathe profile touches the axis at x=0 on both ends, which should just produce harmless degenerate triangles there.

Now I'm working out the vertical positioning so the tower base sinks slightly into the island surface rather than floating above it, adjusting the outline points so the bottom disk starts below zero and tapers up through the correct heights toward the gallery deck level.

Let me lock down the stack of heights more concretely: island top around 2.1, tower rising to world height 12.8, deck spanning 12.6-12.9, railing posts to 13.8, lantern glass to 15.1, then a tapered roof lathe sitting at 15.0 to overlap the glass top slightly, leading into the finial spike base.

I'm sketching out total model height near 16 meters, then planning painted stripes on the tower using a periodic banding function with taper noise so the red bands fade in places for a weathered look. For materials I'm assigning dark iron tones to the deck and railing, and a warm golden hue for the lantern glass, then setting up vertical mullion rods around the lantern at the glass radius.

For the ring placement I need to correct the direction used when offsetting rod endpoints — using raw local coordinates would push the rods outward instead of upward, so I'm switching to a directional "up" offset so the mullions and railing posts rise correctly rather than drifting radially.

Now I'm laying out the lantern's top rail, roof, and finial: a lathed ring near the posts, a red cone roof, and a small dark spike on top for the finial. Then I'm shifting to the cottage structure — positioning a cream-colored box for the walls on the island surface and adding a pyramidal roof rotated to align its faces, followed by planning the door geometry.

I realize the cottage's placement is too close to the central tower's base radius, so I'm moving the cottage further out to roughly x=4.2, z=-2.6 to give clearance, then recalculating the door and window positions on the front face accordingly, placing a dark brown door and two warm-colored windows flush against the wall.

For rocks, I'm scattering dodecahedron boulders around the island's rim using a deterministic random generator, varying angle, radius, size, and rotation so they sit naturally half-submerged at the water's edge in muted gray-brown tones. I'm also adding a large circular water plane beneath the island, tinted a deep blue-teal and rotated flat to serve as the sea surface.

I'm adding a few sphere-based bushes onto the island for extra greenery detail, and noting that since the glass lathe forming the lighthouse lantern housing is solid, there's no need for a separate bright core—its surface alone will carry the visible glass and mullion detailing.

I'm refining the lantern glass with a warm vertical gradient paint and considering a similar striped gradient treatment for the tower, while keeping paint resolutions consistent across all painted parts. I'm also double-checking that the needed builder exports (ring, paint, countershade, stripes, gradient, rng) are all available from the SDK.

For the rocks, water, and railing I'm using primitive Three.js geometries like dodecahedron, circle, and cone shapes through the part builder, applying rotations and positions directly, and setting up a ring of posts with rods for the railing fence.

I'm now working on the mullions and tower structure, using lathe geometry with low segment counts for a faceted low-poly look, defining the island's profile as a series of radius-height points, and setting up countershading colors so the grass-covered top and rocky rim read differently based on their surface normals.

Continuing to lay out the tower's tapered profile and the deck, railing, and roof lathes stacked above it, closing each profile loop carefully so the lathe winding works correctly and picking colors and segment counts for each ring.

Now I'm designing the glass lantern at the tower top with a warm-to-cream vertical gradient, then moving on to the cottage structure—sizing the walls and roof so they nest properly into the island surface, and positioning the door relative to the wall base.

Scattering bushes around the cottage and tower base using sphere geometry placed to match the island's sloped elevation at each point. Writing rock generation loop...

I decide to settle on placing rim rocks at radius 9.8-10.8 with y around 0.15, letting them sit mostly in the water near the island's edge, and skip adding a foam ring to keep things simple. Now I'm checking the imports and types needed—gradient, countershade, stripes functions, the lathe geometry's required point array, and THREE.js for the geometries—to make sure everything will type-check correctly before writing the final code.
